stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 3 weeks of intermittent light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 years ago. She has never used menopausal hormone therapy and takes no other regular medications. She is otherwise well, BMI 27 kg/m2, has never been pregnant, and has no family history of endometrial or ovarian cancer.

You perform a transvaginal ultrasound in the same visit which shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm with a heterogeneous appearance. Both ovaries are quiescent and there is no free fluid. She has no personal history of breast cancer and has never used tamoxifen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable mass; speculum shows a small amount of old blood in the posterior fornix and a smooth pink cervix; bimanual exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 6 mm, heterogeneous; ovaries normal; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to observe any endometrial change over time
options.rationale: Ultrasound alone cannot exclude endometrial cancer once bleeding has occurred and endometrium is above 4 mm; histology is required. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Pipelle endometrial biopsy in the outpatient clinic for histological assessment now
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness above 4 mm on TVS is an indication for endometrial sampling per RANZCOG; Pipelle is the first-line office biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Colposcopy with directed cervical biopsy of any acetowhite areas visualised
options.rationale: Colposcopy assesses cervical disease; the bleeding source here is more likely endometrial and requires endometrial sampling. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Serum CA125 measurement and CT abdomen/pelvis before any tissue diagnosis is sought
options.rationale: CA125 has poor specificity in postmenopausal bleeding and CT is not first-line for endometrial pathology; direct histology is the diagnostic step. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Empirical continuous progestogen without any histological sampling of the endometrium
options.rationale: Treating without diagnosis is unsafe; a proportion of PMB cases represent endometrial carcinoma and require histology first. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding requires exclusion of endometrial carcinoma. RANZCOG uses transvaginal ultrasound as the first-line investigation; endometrial thickness under 4 mm has a very high negative predictive value for carcinoma in a non-tamoxifen user and often needs no further tissue sampling. Thickness of 4 mm or above, heterogeneous appearance, or persistent bleeding despite thin endometrium mandates endometrial biopsy. Pipelle is the outpatient standard; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy follows a failed Pipelle or persistent symptoms with negative sampling. Tamoxifen users get lower ultrasound utility and often go directly to hysteroscopic assessment.
key_points: Endometrial thickness cut-off is 4 mm on TVS for PMB in non tamoxifen users.
Above 4 mm needs Pipelle endometrial biopsy first-line.
Persistent bleeding with thin endometrium still needs hysteroscopy.
Tamoxifen users have reduced TVS utility.
explanation.pearls: In postmenopausal bleeding, an endometrial thickness above 4 mm on TVS mandates Pipelle biopsy in clinic; hysteroscopy follows if Pipelle fails or bleeding persists despite negative histology.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman presents seeking contraception. Her cycles were regular until 12 months ago and are now irregular with heavy bleeding and occasional hot flushes. She has 3 children by uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2, blood pressure is 148/92 on two readings, and she smokes 8 cigarettes a day. She has no personal history of VTE, breast cancer or migraine.

She does not wish to become pregnant, but she is bothered by menstrual heaviness (soaking a pad every 2 hours on the heaviest days) and mild vasomotor symptoms. She has not tried any hormonal method for 20 years. Her partner has had a vasectomy but they have separated and she has a new partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg (repeated), respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 32 kg/m2; abdomen soft with no mass; bimanual pelvic exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-160); ferritin 12 microgram/L (30-160); TSH within normal limits; urine bhCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol 30 microgram and levonorgestrel
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in a woman over 35 who smokes because of unacceptable cardiovascular and VTE risk. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular injection every 12 weeks
options.rationale: DMPA is progestogen-only and safe from a VTE standpoint, but reduces bone mineral density and is less useful for menorrhagia in perimenopause. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system for both contraception and heavy bleeding control
options.rationale: The LNG-IUS provides highly effective contraception, treats heavy menstrual bleeding, and is safe in smokers and those with hypertension; it also acts as endometrial protection if MHT is later added. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Vaginal ring containing ethinylestradiol and etonogestrel replaced every 21 days monthly
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception delivered vaginally still carries the same cardiovascular contraindications in a smoker over 35. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Copper intrauterine device inserted at the earliest opportunity in your consulting rooms
options.rationale: The copper IUD is contraceptive but often worsens heavy menstrual bleeding, which is her primary presenting symptom; a hormonal option is preferred. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

explanation.summary: In a smoker over 35 with hypertension, combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) due to cardiovascular and VTE hazard. Progestogen-only options are safe: the LNG-IUS is first-line when heavy menstrual bleeding coexists, giving 96 percent PBAC reduction and lasting 8 years for both contraception and treatment. DMPA reduces BMD and is less useful for menorrhagia. Copper IUD frequently worsens flow. The LNG-IUS also provides endometrial protection if oestrogen-based MHT is later added for vasomotor symptoms.
key_points: CHC is contraindicated in a smoker over 35 (UKMEC 4).
LNG-IUS combines contraception and menorrhagia treatment.
DMPA reduces bone density with long-term use.
Copper IUD often worsens heavy menstrual bleeding.
explanation.pearls: In perimenopausal smokers with hypertension and heavy periods, the 52 mg LNG-IUS is first choice: contraception, PBAC reduction, and future endometrial protection for MHT in one device.

sources.label: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

subtopic_detail: Suspected ovarian torsion imaging and management
stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 4 hours of sudden onset severe right lower quadrant pain associated with two episodes of vomiting. She reports intermittent similar but milder pain over the past 2 weeks that self-resolved within an hour. She is sexually active with a male partner using condoms; her last menstrual period was 10 days ago and was normal.

On examination she is uncomfortable and tender in the right adnexa without peritonism. A urinary bhCG is negative. Bedside ultrasound in ED shows an enlarged right ovary of 7.2 cm with peripherally displaced follicles and reduced arterial and venous Doppler flow compared with the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; abdomen tender in right iliac fossa and right adnexa without peritonism or guarding; cervix closed on speculum; no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinary bhCG negative; WCC 12.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 14 mg/L (<5); TVS: right ovary 7.2 cm with peripheral follicles and reduced Doppler flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for analgesia and observation with a repeat ultrasound in 12 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Delay increases the risk of irreversible ischaemic ovarian loss; suspected torsion is a surgical emergency and imaging findings already support the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone and doxycycline for empirical pelvic inflammatory disease cover
options.rationale: PID typically features vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness or fever; her picture and imaging fit torsion, and antibiotics do not treat the underlying vascular compromise. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to characterise the adnexal mass further
options.rationale: CT delays theatre without adding to the surgical decision; TVS with Doppler is the imaging modality of choice and is already suggestive. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy and detorsion with ovarian preservation as the primary aim
options.rationale: Clinical picture plus imaging supports adnexal torsion; laparoscopic detorsion within 6 hours preserves ovarian function even if the ovary appears dusky at surgery. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: Oophorectomy at open laparotomy without initial attempt at conservative detorsion
options.rationale: Oophorectomy at the first look loses fertility unnecessarily; RANZCOG supports laparoscopic detorsion first even in a dusky ovary. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency in women of reproductive age. The classical picture is sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain often with vomiting, sometimes preceded by intermittent pain from partial torsion. TVS with Doppler shows an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles and reduced or absent flow; presence of Doppler flow does not exclude torsion. Definitive management is laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation, even if the ovary appears blue-black at surgery, because recovery of function is common. Oophorectomy is reserved for necrosis or when malignancy is suspected.
key_points: TVS with Doppler is first-line imaging; flow presence does not exclude torsion.
Detorsion within 6 hours preserves ovarian function.
Oophorectomy is reserved for necrosis or malignancy.
Cystectomy of any cyst is performed at the same laparoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an enlarged 7 cm ovary and reduced Doppler flow warrants urgent laparoscopy for detorsion; even a dusky ovary should be preserved rather than removed at first look.

stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida is admitted to the day assessment unit at 9+2 weeks with a 3-week history of vomiting more than 8 times daily. She is unable to keep down oral fluids and has lost 4.5 kg from her booking weight of 62 kg (7 percent loss). Urine dipstick is positive for ketones 4+ and specific gravity is 1.030. Serum sodium is 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L.

She has already been prescribed pyridoxine 25 mg TDS and metoclopramide 10 mg TDS in the community for 5 days without benefit. She is not on any other medication. Thyroid function is within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound this morning shows a viable singleton with cardiac activity present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick ketones 4+, specific gravity 1.030; sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.5-7.0); TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition via peripherally inserted central catheter for 2 weeks now
options.rationale: TPN carries VTE, infection and metabolic risks and is a last-line intervention; IV rehydration and antiemetic escalation come first. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Increase metoclopramide to 20 mg oral four times daily and reassess in 48 hours at home
options.rationale: Doubling an already-failed oral antiemetic in a woman who cannot tolerate oral fluids does not address ongoing ketonuria and hypokalaemia. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily as first-line escalation for symptom control
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after failure of standard antiemetics including ondansetron; they are not first-line escalation. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Consider medical termination of pregnancy at 9 weeks to end the underlying trigger
options.rationale: Termination is not an initial management step in refractory nausea; stepwise pharmacological escalation is required first and most women improve into the second trimester. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Admit for IV fluid resuscitation, ondansetron 4 mg IV 8 hourly and thiamine cover
options.rationale: She has failed first-line pyridoxine plus metoclopramide with ketonuria and 7 percent weight loss; admission for IV rehydration, ondansetron and thiamine matches the RANZCOG stepwise algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by persistent vomiting with weight loss over 5 percent, dehydration and ketonuria. First-line is pyridoxine (25 mg 8-hourly) with or without doxylamine. Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or ondansetron are added if symptoms persist; ondansetron is not associated with a meaningful teratogenic signal per contemporary data but is generally reserved for second-line after first-line failure. Refractory disease with electrolyte disturbance requires admission for IV fluids, thiamine and IV antiemetics; corticosteroids or TPN are last-line options.
key_points: First-line: pyridoxine +/- doxylamine.
Second-line: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or ondansetron.
Admission if 5 percent weight loss, ketonuria or failed oral therapy.
Thiamine cover before IV dextrose to prevent Wernicke.
explanation.pearls: HG that has failed pyridoxine + metoclopramide with ketonuria and 7 percent weight loss needs admission for IV Hartmann's plus ondansetron plus thiamine; steroids come only if IV antiemetics fail.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Obstetrics - Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

stem:
A 30-year-old woman (G3P2) attends the antenatal clinic at 34 weeks to discuss her mode of delivery. Her first delivery was an emergency lower segment caesarean section for foetal distress at 8 cm dilatation at term. Her second delivery was an uncomplicated elective repeat lower segment caesarean at 39 weeks. She now wishes to attempt a vaginal birth after caesarean.

Her operative notes describe a low transverse uterine incision at both prior surgeries with no extension. She has a healthy singleton foetus in cephalic presentation, estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile, and adequate liquor. She has no other maternal medical problems. This antenatal clinic uses continuous intrapartum foetal monitoring and can offer immediate caesarean recovery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, foetal heart rate 138/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 34 cm; foetus cephalic; abdomen soft; scar Pfannenstiel well-healed
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 32 weeks: cephalic, EFW 55th centile, normal liquor; previous operative notes: two low transverse incisions without extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Offer planned VBAC with continuous CTG monitoring in labour and one-to-one midwifery care
options.rationale: With two low transverse caesareans, a stable current pregnancy, cephalic presentation and no other contraindications, VBAC can be offered with informed consent, continuous CTG and immediate access to caesarean recovery. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Two prior caesareans is an absolute contraindication and mandates elective caesarean now
options.rationale: Two prior low transverse caesareans is not an absolute contraindication in RANZCOG guidance; VBAC after two caesareans can be considered with informed counselling. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Recommend induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel and titrated oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction in a woman with a scarred uterus is associated with substantially increased rupture risk and is generally avoided. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Recommend home birth given her strong preference for a vaginal birth in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Prior caesarean is a contraindication to planned home birth in Australia because emergency caesarean access is essential for scar rupture management. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Arrange elective classical uterine incision caesarean at 37 weeks for safer scar assessment
options.rationale: A classical (vertical) incision is not indicated when previous incisions were low transverse and carries much higher rupture risk in future pregnancies. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

explanation.summary: Planned VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean) can be offered after one or two prior low transverse caesareans with informed consent, continuous CTG monitoring in labour, and access to immediate caesarean recovery. Absolute contraindications include prior classical or T-shaped uterine incision, prior uterine rupture, and some contraindications to any vaginal delivery (major placenta praevia, transverse lie unrelieved). Induction with prostaglandins is discouraged due to scar rupture risk; mechanical methods (Foley) or oxytocin alone are preferred. Success rates approach 70 percent overall and 90 percent when a previous vaginal birth occurred.
key_points: One or two prior low transverse caesareans is not an absolute contraindication.
Classical or T-shaped incision is an absolute contraindication.
Prostaglandin induction carries increased rupture risk on a scarred uterus.
Home birth is contraindicated after prior caesarean.
explanation.pearls: Two prior low transverse caesareans with a well-positioned cephalic foetus is a legitimate VBAC candidate in Australia, with counselling, continuous CTG and prompt caesarean access; avoid prostaglandin induction.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Vaginal birth after caesarean

stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida presents in spontaneous labour at 39+4 weeks with regular painful uterine contractions every 3 minutes. Her membranes are intact and cervical dilatation is 5 cm on admission. Her antenatal course was uncomplicated. Her low vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks returned positive for Streptococcus agalactiae.

She is not allergic to any medications. Her booking group and hold is O positive with negative antibody screen. She has no personal or family history of anaphylaxis. Her partner is present and she is coping well with the contractions. The registrar is preparing an IV cannula.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, foetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, fully effaced, foetal head at 0 station; membranes intact; regular contractions every 3 minutes lasting 40 seconds
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab at 36 weeks positive for Streptococcus agalactiae; no other positive cultures; no drug allergy documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic plan?

options.text: IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 hours to cover both penicillin allergy and resistant GBS
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for penicillin-allergic women at high risk of anaphylaxis with clindamycin resistance; she has no allergy. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery of the baby
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is first-line intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in Australia when there is no allergy; loading is 3 g IV then 1.8 g 4-hourly until delivery. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days commenced now during her labour
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate placental transfer within labour timeframes; IV therapy is required for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until membranes rupture or 18 hours from onset elapse in labour
options.rationale: Prophylaxis should begin as soon as labour is established in a known GBS carrier; delay reduces the duration of therapeutic maternal levels before delivery. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus

options.text: IV cefazolin 2 g load then 1 g every 8 hours to cover any beta-lactam concerns preemptively
options.rationale: Cefazolin is second-line for penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis risk; she is not allergic and benzylpenicillin remains first-line. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus

explanation.summary: Australian intrapartum GBS prophylaxis follows a risk-based/screening hybrid approach. Women with a positive late-gestation swab, prior GBS-affected infant, or GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy receive intrapartum prophylaxis starting when labour is established or membranes rupture. Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading dose then 1.8 g 4-hourly is first-line. Cefazolin covers penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis risk. Clindamycin is used if resistance testing is confirmed and allergy is severe; vancomycin is reserved for anaphylaxis with clindamycin resistance.
key_points: First-line: benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g 4-hourly.
Cefazolin for penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis.
Clindamycin if severe allergy and susceptibility documented.
Adequate coverage is 4 hours before delivery.
explanation.pearls: GBS-positive woman in established labour with no allergy: start IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g 4-hourly at first opportunity; aim for at least 4 hours of coverage before delivery.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus
RANZCOG maternal group B streptococcus disease guideline
